details:
Versions 0.1.0-beta through 0.1.8-beta export `useTerminal`, a server-side middleware factory that stands up a WebSocket-to-PTY bridge with no authentication on the upgrade path. The package's main entry (`dist/index.js`) is a barrel of roughly 37 UI components, and `useTerminal` is exported alongside them.

Mechanism (`dist/useTerminal.js` — byte-identical across 0.1.0-beta through 0.1.5-beta, modified but still unauthenticated in 0.1.6-beta, 0.1.7-beta and 0.1.8-beta): the factory creates `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })` and returns Express-style `(req, res, next)` middleware. When a request matches the default path `/terminal-stream` and carries an `Upgrade: websocket` header, the middleware calls `wss.handleUpgrade(...)` with no token check, no `Origin` check and no host or loopback restriction (0.1.8-beta: `dist/useTerminal.js:128-132`). On the first `init` message the connection handler calls `pty.spawn(shell, shellArgs, { cwd: process.env.HOME || os.homedir(), env: { ...process.env, TERM: 'xterm-256color' } })`, where `shell` defaults to `bash` with `['-i']` on POSIX and `powershell.exe` on Windows. Later messages are written straight into the PTY via `session.ptyProcess.write(parsed.data)`, and a `catch (_)` fallback writes raw non-JSON message bytes to the PTY as well. PTY output is streamed back over the socket. `dist/terminal.js` ships the matching browser client, which connects to the same path and sends keystrokes as `{type:'input', data:...}`, so the package carries both ends of the channel.

Exposure and preconditions: no version declares a `preinstall`, `install`, `postinstall` or `prepare` script, and nothing executes at module scope — the server is constructed with `noServer: true` and cannot bind a port on its own. Reaching the shell requires the consuming application to mount the exported middleware on a listening server. Where it is mounted and network-reachable, any unauthenticated client can obtain an interactive shell running as the server process, with that process's full environment and the user's home directory as the working directory. The affected range contains no outbound network calls, no obfuscation, and no access to credential files.

Remediation: 0.1.9-beta authenticates ahead of the upgrade — the middleware reads a token from an `Authorization: Bearer` header or a `terminal-token.` WebSocket subprotocol, compares it using `crypto.timingSafeEqual` behind a length pre-check, and returns HTTP 401 before `handleUpgrade` on mismatch; `useTerminal()` also throws at construction when no token is configured, so it cannot be instantiated unauthenticated. 0.2.0-beta adds origin allowlisting, loopback restriction and per-session ownership; 0.2.1-beta and 0.2.2-beta extend this further. 0.1.9-beta and later are not affected.

Affected-version correction: 0.1.8-beta is affected and was absent from the original record, which enumerated 0.1.0-beta through 0.1.7-beta only. It was confirmed by reading `dist/useTerminal.js` (sha256 `d0039deadf22124cfeb9ffc919961f641b020e478348f82dd24956b9b340d53b`) in the published 0.1.8-beta artifact, where `handleUpgrade` is still reached with no authentication. No IN-MAL finding ID exists for 0.1.8-beta; it was added by manual analysis, so it does not appear in the per-source origins below.

## Source: amazon-inspector (b8497bfe55fd379ac7c87c73e99e8c532193a17516996d9ae6cfb856b84a052a)
The package advertises itself as a UI-components library (README compares it to MUI), but its main export surface includes `useTerminal`, a server-side middleware that stands up a WebSocketServer (default path `/terminal-stream`) and, on every incoming WS message, spawns an interactive bash/powershell PTY via `pty.spawn` with the server process's own environment (`{...process.env, TERM: 'xterm-256color'}`) and cwd set to the user's home directory. Bytes received from the WebSocket are written directly into the PTY (`session.ptyProcess.write(parsed.data)`, with a fallback that writes raw message bytes), and PTY output is streamed back to the socket. No authentication, origin check, or handshake token gates the connection. `dist/terminal.js` ships the matching browser client (exported as `Terminal`) that connects to that same WebSocket and pipes keystrokes as `{type:'input', data:...}`, so the package ships both ends of a remote-shell channel. A consumer who mounts the exported hook — expecting a UI helper — exposes a full unauthenticated interactive shell on their server, executing as the server process. The mismatch between the marketed purpose (UI kit) and the shipped capability (network-driven RCE) is the shape of a backdoor delivered under a benign cover story.
